oneLineDefinition: The study of how individuals, firms, and governments allocate scarce resources, and how these decisions shape markets, prices, and economic outcomes.
overview: Economics studies decision-making under scarcity at every level — from individual consumer choices to national monetary policy. It has two main branches: microeconomics (individual agents, markets, prices) and macroeconomics (GDP, inflation, employment, trade). Modern economics is increasingly quantitative — using statistics, econometrics, and data to test theories. In Vietnam, Economics graduates work in government agencies, banks, research institutes, and increasingly in data-driven private sector roles.
typicalProjects: Run a regression analysis on household income and consumption data
Write a policy brief on the impact of minimum wage changes
Analyze Vietnam's trade data and identify structural patterns
Model the effect of a tax change on market equilibrium
Conduct a cost-benefit analysis of a public infrastructure investment
requiredSkills: Mathematical reasoning — especially optimization and statistical thinking
Ability to construct and test hypotheses with data
Reading and synthesizing economic research (largely in English)
Comfort with abstract model-building before applying to real data
suitableFor: Students who enjoy understanding why markets and policies work the way they do
Those with mathematical aptitude who also want to engage with social and political questions
Students interested in research, policy, or data-driven advisory roles
Those considering graduate school or research careers
notSuitableFor: Students who dislike abstract mathematical modeling
Those who want a practical, immediately job-ready curriculum
Students who are not interested in reading dense English-language research
keyTakeaways: Modern economics requires quantitative skills — econometrics and data analysis are not optional
The degree is highly transferable: economists work in finance, government, tech, consulting, and research
Graduate school (Master's or PhD) significantly expands career options in research and policy
Econometrics skills (Stata, R, Python) make economics graduates competitive in data-heavy roles
cautionNotes: Economics theory can feel disconnected from immediate practical application — patience with abstraction is required
Programs in Vietnam vary significantly in rigor — some are more theory-heavy, others more applied
Graduates competing for finance or banking roles face strong competition from Finance & Banking majors
careerPaths: Economist at central bank or ministry
marketDemand: Moderate in Vietnam for pure economics roles. Higher demand for graduates who combine economics with quantitative or digital skills. Government and financial sector are the largest hirers.
salaryOutlook: Entry-level government or research roles earn 8–15M VND/month. Private sector roles (banking, consulting, data) earn 15–30M. Senior economists and policy advisors at top institutions earn significantly more.
futureTrend: Computational economics and data-driven policy analysis are growing. Economists with Python/R and causal inference skills are increasingly valued in tech companies and financial institutions.
commonMisconceptions: Economics is about the stock market — most economics is about broader resource allocation, policy, and market theory, not just financial markets
Economics is purely theoretical — applied and behavioral economics are highly data-driven fields
You need to study economics to understand business — business decisions draw on economics but the two degrees have different emphases

faq.question: Is Economics better than Finance & Banking for a career in banking?
faq.answer: Finance & Banking is more directly job-ready for commercial banking roles. Economics provides a stronger theoretical and quantitative foundation, which is better for research, central banking, or roles requiring macroeconomic analysis. For corporate banking and credit roles, Finance is more practical; for policy or research roles, Economics is stronger.
